title: Hormuz Reopening Deal Imminent as Oman Mediates, Ukraine Escalates Drone War Deep Into Russia, Israel-Lebanon Talks Enter Seventh Round
subhead: US and Iranian officials signal a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come within days, oil prices fell sharply on the news. Ukraine struck Wildberries warehouses near Moscow while Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles. Israel and Lebanon opened a seventh round of talks in Rome.

sections.heading: Hormuz Reopening Nears as Oman-Mediated Talks Progress
sections.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at the State Department on Tuesday that 'progress has been made' in discussions between Oman and Iran on establishing safe shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz, though 'there is no finality yet.' Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was more specific, telling CNBC that a deal to reopen the strait could be agreed 'today or tomorrow,' describing it as enabling 'freedom of movement' for commercial vessels.

Iran continues to deny direct negotiations with Washington. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran is talking only with Oman, the mediator, and that those discussions had been 'positive' at both political and technical levels. Outstanding issues reportedly include the mechanism for transits, maritime service fees, and security arrangements.

According to a former Pentagon official cited by Al Jazeera, the rough outline of a deal would involve Iran restricting passage through its territorial waters while allowing free transit through Omani waters — effectively negating the traditional right of innocent passage but keeping commercial traffic flowing. Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani spoke with President Trump on Tuesday, praising Doha's mediation role.

Oil prices dropped sharply on the news. Brent crude fell almost 5 percent to under $80 a barrel, its lowest since July 13, while US West Texas Intermediate dropped more than 5 percent to $76. The previous day, Trump had warned Iran it faced its 'last chance' to agree to a deal.
sections.whyItMatters: A Hormuz reopening would be the most significant de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict since the June memorandum of understanding. Global oil supplies and prices — already battered by months of disruption — hang in the balance.

sections.heading: Ukraine-Russia Escalation: Deep Strikes and Civilian Targeting
sections.body:
Ukraine dramatically expanded its drone campaign inside Russia overnight Monday, hitting at least three facilities operated by Wildberries — Russia's largest online retailer, often described as the 'Russian Amazon' — in the Moscow, St Petersburg, and Tver regions. At least five people were killed and 10 injured at an industrial site 69km south of the Kremlin, according to local officials. A Wildberries warehouse in the Samara region hit on Sunday was completely destroyed, Russian state media reported.

Ukraine says the depots supply the Russian military. Russia's defence ministry said it intercepted 320 drones overnight. The strikes followed a drone attack on a beach in the Krasnodar region on Monday that killed seven people and injured 58, according to Russian officials.

On Wednesday, Russia launched ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, killing at least one woman and wounding 12 others. Kyiv's military administration chief Timur Tkachenko said residential buildings and warehouses were hit. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said people may be trapped under rubble.

Ukraine also published video of a Russian drone pursuing a 52-year-old vegetable vendor named Yuriy through the streets of Kherson — what Ukraine calls 'human safari' attacks on civilians. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called it a 'barbaric war crime' and part of a deliberate strategy of civilian intimidation. A 2025 UN report found Russian forces 'recurrently killed and injured civilians' through such drone attacks.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's strikes deep into Russia — targeting commercial logistics infrastructure near Moscow — mark a significant escalation in reach. Simultaneously, Russia's continued targeting of civilians in front-line areas, documented on video, underscores the war's enduring brutality and the deepening stalemate.

sections.heading: Ceuta Crisis Recedes as EU Praises Spain's Response
sections.body:
EU interior ministers met in Brussels on Tuesday and broadly endorsed Spain's handling of the Ceuta migrant crisis. EU Commissioner Magnus Brunner called it a 'test' of European resilience that had been 'passed.' Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said approximately 70,000 of the estimated 72,000 people who crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30-31 have been returned to Morocco. At least 75 people died on the Spanish side and 11 in Morocco.

Italy had suspended its Schengen agreement with Spain last week, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni calling the images 'shocking' and a security threat. Denmark and Finland backed Italy's move, and 22 EU nations signed a letter of concern. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez pushed back, noting that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen area and accusing critics of acting from 'prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest.' Grande-Marlaska said the Schengen zone had not been compromised and urged Italy to lift added controls 'as soon as possible.'

The EU offered Spain emergency financial support. Spain has allocated roughly 25 million euros for the care of unaccompanied minors — approximately 800 children — still in Ceuta. The crisis was reportedly triggered by a Spanish Supreme Court ruling barring summary returns of migrants stopped at sea, combined with social media-fuelled disinformation.
sections.whyItMatters: While the immediate crisis is easing, the political fallout is exposing deep fractures in the EU over migration policy. Italy's Schengen suspension and the 22-nation letter of concern signal that Ceuta's lessons will shape European border politics for months to come.

sections.heading: Israel-Lebanon Talks Resume in Rome Amid Continued Strikes
sections.body:
A seventh round of US-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon opened in Rome on Tuesday, focused on establishing new 'pilot zones' in southern Lebanon from which Israeli forces would withdraw and the Lebanese army would assume security control. Lebanon's delegation includes former ambassador to the US Simon Karam and current ambassador Nada Mouawad, along with Brigadier-General George Rizkallah leading the military team.

Under the June 26 framework deal, Israel agreed to 'progressively redeploy' from the roughly 20 percent of Lebanese territory it occupies, in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah. The first pilot zone withdrawal took place in July, but Israel continues to hold a 10km buffer zone — what it calls the 'Yellow Line' — and says it will remain until Hezbollah disarms.

Even as talks proceeded, Lebanon's state news agency reported that Israeli forces dropped phosphorus bombs on olive groves in Yaroun, Arnoun, and Bint Jbeil, causing fires. An Israeli drone also dropped a stun grenade in Bayt al-Sayyad near Tyre. Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem denounced the negotiations, calling them a source of 'shame, humiliation, disappointment and constant concessions' for Lebanon. Over 4,000 people have been killed in Lebanon since the Israel-Hezbollah war began in March.
sections.whyItMatters: Seven rounds of talks have produced incremental progress but no breakthrough. With Israel occupying a fifth of Lebanon and Hezbollah rejecting the process entirely, the gap between diplomatic frameworks and on-the-ground reality continues to widen.

sections.heading: Argentina Grain Ports Paralyzed as Pilots Strike Over Milei Decree
sections.body:
Maritime pilots in Argentina walked off the job on Monday after President Javier Milei's government published a decree deregulating river navigation services. The decree aims to 'streamline procedures' and 'eliminate obsolete regulations,' but the pilots' union says it threatens their jobs and the safety of river traffic. At least 45 vessels are currently stuck at Argentine ports, and the chamber of export businesses CIARA-CEC warned that 30 more ships would be affected each day the strike continues.

Argentina is the world's largest exporter of soya bean products and a major corn and wheat supplier. Any prolonged disruption at its Parana River ports — the conduit for most of its agricultural exports — ripples through global food markets, which are already stressed by the Hormuz and Red Sea shipping crises.

Argentina's coastguard on Tuesday ordered the pilots back to work, threatening disciplinary sanctions. It remains to be seen whether the order will be enforced. The country ratified the EU-Mercosur trade deal in February with a 69-3 Senate vote, and the strike comes at a delicate moment for that agreement's implementation.
sections.whyItMatters: With global shipping already under strain from Hormuz and Red Sea disruptions, a prolonged Argentine grain port shutdown compounds pressure on food supply chains — particularly for developing nations dependent on soya imports.

sections.heading: Red Sea Security Deteriorates as Indian Ship Sinks Off Yemen
sections.body:
An Indian-flagged vessel, the MSV Faize Noore Oliya, was struck by a projectile and sank off the coast of Yemen on Tuesday. All 14 crew members — 13 of them Indian nationals — were rescued by the Yemeni coastguard. India's Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal condemned the 'unprovoked attack.' Yemen's internationally recognized government blamed the Iran-backed Houthis, saying the attack was carried out using a boat laden with explosives. The Houthis have not commented.

The incident is the latest in a series of attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea, which had become a crucial alternative route for oil tankers since Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz in February. The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports on July 20 and have since claimed attacks on oil tankers, commercial shipping, and energy infrastructure — including a drone strike on Najran airport in southern Saudi Arabia that disrupted operations by damaging the facility's main radar system.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has reported multiple attacks on ships in the region over the past week. The dual blockage of Hormuz and the Houthi campaign in the Red Sea has created what analysts describe as a near-total disruption of Middle Eastern oil export routes, with cascading effects on global fuel prices.
sections.whyItMatters: The Red Sea was supposed to be the workaround for Hormuz. With Houthi attacks now sinking ships outright, there is no safe alternative route for Middle Eastern oil — making a Hormuz reopening deal all the more urgent.

bottomLine: The most consequential development today is the possibility — still fragile and contested — of a Hormuz reopening deal within days, mediated by Oman. Oil markets responded immediately, with Brent dropping below $80. But the path ahead is littered with complications: Iran denies direct talks with the US, Red Sea shipping is under active attack by Houthis, and past ceasefire attempts have collapsed within weeks. Meanwhile, the Ukraine-Russia war escalated on both fronts, with Ukraine striking deep into Russia and Russia hitting Kyiv with ballistic missiles. Seven rounds of Israel-Lebanon talks have yet to produce a meaningful ceasefire. And Argentina's grain ports are suddenly offline, adding a food supply shock to an already disrupted global trade picture.
